French feminist icon Gisèle Pelicot, who became a worldwide symbol against sexual violence during the 2024 rape trials against her husband and dozens of other men, said Monday she will take legal action after nude images of her were sent out without her permission to publicise a psychoanalyst's book on coercive control.

Finland on Monday said it had summoned Russia's ambassador over a suspected violation of Finnish airspace by a Russian helicopter and after a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian cargo ship located in the Gulf of Finland in recent days. Helsinki also condemned Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7ad57222-e759-11f1-9bc1-e56ab3dc0809/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26326490305591.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7ad57222-e759-11f1-9bc1-e56ab3dc0809/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26326490305591.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">54a67868-e758-11f1-86b6-1b6ab457b0a3</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:50:41 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/7ad57222-e759-11f1-9bc1-e56ab3dc0809/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26326490305591.jpg">© Finnish Border Guard/Lehtikuva via AP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item><item><title>🔴Democrats vow probe after Trump admits role in Huang's return as Nvidia CEO</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/americas/20261123-nvidia-board-reinstates-disgraced-jensen-huang-as-ceo-president-says</link><description></description><guid isPermaLink="false">11d14884-e75c-11f1-8499-6d6e1e58e668</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:37:04 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>Airports, public transport shut down amid national strike in Belgium</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261123-airports-public-transport-shut-down-amid-national-strike-in-belgium</link><description>
Belgium's prime minister on Monday set a new year-end deadline for his coalition government to agree a cost-cutting budget or face collapse. The announcement came as a national strike against the planned cuts grounded all flights in and out of Belgium. Public transport, schools and other public services also faced disruption. France 24's Dave Keating has the latest from Brussels.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d81660fe-e754-11f1-aa59-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261123-161537-161925-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d81660fe-e754-11f1-aa59-1bac47ab2f5d/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261123-161537-161925-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">dd0a6d58-e754-11f1-8f83-1f392e0d452d</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:10:30 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>Asia / Pacific</category><title>Iran's courts order US to pay $290 billion in damages</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/iran-s-courts-order-us-to-pay-290-billion-in-damages</link><description>
Iranian courts have ordered the United States to pay $290 billion in damages for decades of US actions against the Islamic Republic, a judiciary official said Monday. He added that lawsuits have also been filed against Gulf Arab states accused of letting Washington use their territory to strike Iran.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">c1631b3e-e751-11f1-941c-6b60b041de3b</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 15:50:11 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/d7a75eea-1b1f-11f1-86b4-005056bfb2b6/w:1024/p:16x9/AP26067484115759.jpg">© Alireza Sotakbar, AP</source><dc:creator>FRANCE 24</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work ]]> Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics. The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation, the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut.

Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field.

As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.

The rules change when gravity disappears

We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well.

"First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author.

"'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen."

In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height.

Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude.

Of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with maneuvering yourself. Any ball or other object would also be subject to this altered set of physics.

As Johnson points out, "Aside from maneuvering the body and not tumbling or going in the wrong direction, the most difficult part would probably be throwing or hitting a ball in zero g. There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw. That would take getting used to doing, given that we’ve spent our entire lives calculating how high and fast to throw a ball in 1G so it gets to the person we intend."

Science fiction interpretations have often leaned into these differences; in many cases, low-g sports look more like three-dimensional chess than the highly physical contests we're used to here on Earth.

Zero‑g competition in sci‑fi worlds

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

2013's "Ender's Game" gives us one of the best examples of a zero-g arena in space. Dubbed the "Battle Room," it's a giant hollow cube filled with obstacles. Teams enter through gates at opposite ends and participate in laser tag-style drills while having to grapple with three-dimensional space, while also finding ways to propel and protect themselves.

"The Battle Room sequence does a great job of thinking about straight‑line, constant‑velocity motion," Johnson said. "No 'reaction' to slow you down or change your direction. Characters push off walls or each other, then drift until they hit something or fire their suit's thrusters."

Johnson said Ender's Game also did an admirable job of showcasing how alternate physics require another layer of planning when moving through space.

"They went to great lengths to show that there was no preferred 'up' or 'down'. Again, very accurate and realistic thinking. Floating obstacles in the battle space created realistic constraints: if you don't think about where you'll rebound, you can pin yourself behind an obstacle or drift out of the fight."

Real proposals for space sports

Recognizing how important play can be (and, perhaps, acknowledging ways to combat the lingering specter of space madness), real-world space agencies have begun brainstorming what recreation in low gravity might look like. Some proposed ideas include 3D ball games not wholly dissimilar from the Battle Room, where players enter a cube or spherical arena and push off walls/pass a ball in any direction, scoring by hitting targets.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. The Space Games Federation has also floated the idea of a version of space basketball, where the goal is guiding a magnetic ball through hoops, as well as some version of space dodgeball.

Of course, these proposals are nothing more than thought exercises at the moment. We're a long way out from vast human populations living in zero-g environments for extended periods of time, and even further still from building spaceships capable of housing a sports hall.

NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

These fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need new rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Where sci‑fi gets it right (and wrong) about space sports

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

The game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs."

With that said, there are areas where sci-fi portrayals of zero-G games fall down. Energy levels and fatigue is a big one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the issue of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how quickly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." He points to incidents where real-life astronauts have demonstrated how challenging this phenomenon would actually be. "I’ve watched many videos of astronauts on the ISS twist and then bounce off the wall or something. They have all looked very clumsy when they do this."

The other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that said, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

These fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need new rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Where sci‑fi gets it right (and wrong) about space sports

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

The game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs."

Energy levels and fatigue is a big one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the issue of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how quickly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." The other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that said, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

]]> <![CDATA[ Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance ]]> NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

]]> <![CDATA[ The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026 ]]>

Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.

What is it?

The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.

This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.

Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers).

Why is it incredible?

While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported.

In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material.

The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past.

By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

]]> <![CDATA[ What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars? ]]> On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Last of the Soviet space explorers

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues.

Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

Unexplained failure

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

Achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

Theories involving the failure

Although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

The shadow in Phobos 2's final photos

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

Among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

Given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Explaining the Phobos "shadow"

Determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature."

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

However, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The legacy of the Soviet Phobos missions

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

John M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

"The scientific community is also facing challenges resulting from the restructuring of the Soviet system," the Times also reported, noting the scientists from more than a dozen nations around the world whose funding and scientific instruments, at an estimated cost of several millions of dollars, "must be counted among the losers in the failure of the probe to complete its basic mission."

Although both Phobos spacecraft were lost prior to completion of their primary missions, there were still some meaningful scientific results they produced. These included new data collected about both Mars and Phobo­s which, according to Ulivi and Harland, exceeded the total data collected from all past Soviet missions to the Red Planet.

Ultimately, the circumstances surrounding the demise of Phobos 2 remain one of the more intriguing episodes in the history of Soviet space exploration. The unusual observations made during its final moments, coupled with lingering questions about precisely what went wrong, have helped sustain decades of speculation.

Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g)
Bulb type: Non-specified
Laser: No
Control: On-unit
Rotation: Yes, one speed

It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

"We were actually looking for planets," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement. "Instead, we found something much more surprising."

So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years. Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here."

This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects.

A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity. This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across.

Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass.

Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly.

One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual.

SPIRou discovers planets by measuring how much their gravity tugs on their host star. Think of a star and planet orbiting a kind of gravitational balancing point between them called a center of mass. This center of mass is usually inside the star, since the star is far more massive than the planet, but crucially not at its very center, so the star appears to wobble to and fro around the combined center of mass.

The spectrometer measures this wobble in the form of a Doppler shift in the star's light that can be translated into the velocity at which the star is moving around this center of mass. Astronomers call this a 'radial velocity'. A large gas giant like Jupiter might incur a radial velocity of hundreds of meters per second, while an Earth-mass planet generates a radial velocity of tens of meters.

Amazon's first satellite launch since a rocket failure doomed 40 of its spacecraft is set for Tuesday morning (Nov. 24), and you can watch the action live.

An Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation is scheduled to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, on Tuesday (Nov. 23), during a 29-minute window that opens at 5:45 a.m. EST (1045 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time in Kourou). You can watch it live here at Space.com courtesy of Arianespace, the French company that operates the Ariane 6.

The launch was originally supposed to take place on Monday (Nov. 23), but that attempt was scrubbed due to a technical issue affecting the rocket's ground support systems, according to Arianespace.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's New Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And New Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

The Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

The upcoming mission will be the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year.

Vrtulník transportoval zraněného do nemocnice</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/906526-srazka-dodavky-a-kamionu-v-provodine-vrtulnik-transportoval-zraneneho-do-nemocnice.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/906526-srazka-dodavky-a-kamionu-v-provodine-vrtulnik-transportoval-zraneneho-do-nemocnice.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 20:09:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>K nehodě dodávky a nákladního auta v Provodíně na Českolipsku vyjížděly dnes ve 12:13 dvě jednotky profesionálních hasičů. Ze zdemolované dodávky museli vyprostit zaklíněného člověka, kterého následně letecká záchranná služba přepravila do libereckého traumacentra.</description></item><item><title>Tohle byste na autě nechtěli. Žena vylila na BMW omáčku, vadilo jí, kde parkuje</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/906518-tohle-byste-na-aute-nechteli-zena-vylila-na-bmw-omacku-vadilo-ji-kde-parkuje.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/krimi/906518-tohle-byste-na-aute-nechteli-zena-vylila-na-bmw-omacku-vadilo-ji-kde-parkuje.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Krimi</category><description>V pátek 20. listopadu odpoledne vyjížděli jablonečtí strážníci do Pivovarské ulice k bizarnímu případu. Někdo tam vylil na čelní sklo zaparkovaného BMW neznámou tekutinu, ze které se vyklubala hnědá omáčka.</description></item><item><title>Liberec musí v plaveckém areálu opravit i střechu nad malým bazénem</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906487-liberec-musi-v-plaveckem-arealu-opravit-i-strechu-nad-malym-bazenem.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906487-liberec-musi-v-plaveckem-arealu-opravit-i-strechu-nad-malym-bazenem.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:00:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Liberec bude muset na plaveckém stadionu opravit i střechu přístavby s pětadvacetimetrovým bazénem. Městský areál je kvůli modernizaci za více než 800 milionů bez daně uzavřený už dva roky. Práce by měly skončit za rok, ale s opravou přístavby město nepočítalo.</description></item><item><title>Plynaři zkontrolují před mrazy těsnost plynovodů, zápach plynu zesílí</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906264-plynari-zkontroluji-pred-mrazy-tesnost-plynovodu-zapach-plynu-zesili.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906264-plynari-zkontroluji-pred-mrazy-tesnost-plynovodu-zapach-plynu-zesili.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 16:45:00 +0100</pubDate><category>Společnost</category><description>Skupina GasNet, největší distributor plynu v České republice, od pondělí 23. do pátku 27. listopadu dočasně zvyšuje intenzitu zápachu dodávaného zemního plynu. Nárazová odorizace probíhá každoročně před vrcholem topné sezony a zásadním způsobem přispívá k bezpečnému provozu plynárenských zařízení.</description></item><item><title>Vánoční strom na Staromáku pochází z Liberce. Ozdobí jej obří světelná mašle</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906453-vanocni-strom-na-staromaku-ozdobi-obri-svetelna-masle-novinka-poslouzi-i-jako-fotokoutek.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906453-vanocni-strom-na-staromaku-ozdobi-obri-svetelna-masle-novinka-poslouzi-i-jako-fotokoutek.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 14:55:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Barbora Genser</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Praha už zná podobu letošního vánočního stromu na Staroměstském náměstí. Smrk z libereckých Šimonovic byl v sobotu pokácen a zamířil na cestu do centra metropole. Největší novinkou letošní výzdoby bude čtyřmetrová 3D světelná mašle, která zároveň poslouží jako netradiční fotokoutek.</description></item><item><title>Liberečtí šermíři byli 81 let bez zázemí. Teď vybírají na svůj první sál</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906479-liberecti-sermiri-byli-81-let-bez-zazemi-ted-vybiraji-na-svuj-prvni-sal.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906479-liberecti-sermiri-byli-81-let-bez-zazemi-ted-vybiraji-na-svuj-prvni-sal.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 12:40:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Vychovávají mládežnické reprezentanty, přesto už osm desetiletí jen kočují po pronájmech. Šerm Liberec, z. s. konečně staví vlastní zázemí v Truhlářské ulici v Liberci, které bude dětem otevřené nonstop. S vybavením nového sálu teď můžete oddílu pomoct ve sbírce na Donio.cz.</description></item><item><title>Promenádní cestu u přehrady v Liberci otevře město nejdřív v prosinci</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906452-promenadni-cestu-u-prehrady-v-liberci-otevre-mesto-nejdriv-v-prosinci.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906452-promenadni-cestu-u-prehrady-v-liberci-otevre-mesto-nejdriv-v-prosinci.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 11:20:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Oblíbenou promenádní cestu u přehrady v Liberci otevře město nejdřív v prosinci. Práce mají několikaměsíční zpoždění a město za úpravu okolí vodního díla zaplatí bezmála 90 milionů korun. Původně radnice počítala s částkou pod 80 milionů.</description></item><item><title>Poděkování fanouškům, absolutorium hráčům. Trenér Fodrek byl po Spartě spokojený</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906461-podekovani-fanouskum-absolutorium-hracum-trener-fodrek-byl-po-sparte-spokojeny.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/fotbal/906461-podekovani-fanouskum-absolutorium-hracum-trener-fodrek-byl-po-sparte-spokojeny.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 09:55:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Fotbal</category><description>Ani po výhře 3:1 na Spartě u trenéra Slovanu Branislava Fodreka nebyl vidět úsměv. Z jeho slov ale plynulo, že byl hodně spokojený, hráče chválil a děkoval i početné výpravě hostujících fanoušků. Sám ale mluvil o tom, že jeho tým na podzim čekají ještě čtyři další těžké zápasy.</description></item><item><title>V Libereckém kraji nasněžilo, silničáři radí opatrnost</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906448-v-libereckem-kraji-nasnezilo-a-misty-stale-snezi-silnicari-radi-opatrnost.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906448-v-libereckem-kraji-nasnezilo-a-misty-stale-snezi-silnicari-radi-opatrnost.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 08:33:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>ČTK</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>V Libereckém kraji do rána nasněžilo a místy se stále objevují sněhové přeháňky, silnice jsou s opatrností sjízdné. Hlavní tahy jsou většinou jen holé a mokré, pozor by si měli dát řidiči v horských oblastech, kde může na silnicích ležet rozbředlý sníh.</description></item><item><title>Někdo ho vyhodil jako odpad. Malé kotě Bambi zachránila z kontejneru všímavá žena</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906414-nekdo-ho-vyhodil-jako-odpad-male-kote-bambi-zachranila-z-kontejneru-vsimava-zena.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/906414-nekdo-ho-vyhodil-jako-odpad-male-kote-bambi-zachranila-z-kontejneru-vsimava-zena.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 23 Nov 2026 06:30:00 +0100</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Tiché mňoukání z téměř prázdného kontejneru zachránilo v České Lípě život malému kotěti. Na pomoc zvířeti, které tam s největší pravděpodobností někdo úmyslně odložil, zavolala kolemjdoucí žena strážníky. Kočičí holčička Bambi nyní bojuje se zdravotními potížemi v útulku.</description></item></channel></rss>

výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu dobrý den ze šluknovského výběžku, konce světa - šluknovský výběžek Mon, 23 Nov 2026 19:20:55 +0000 cs hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.5 https://www.vybezek.eu/wp-uploads/2018/09/cropped-favicon-vybezek-32x32.png výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu 32 32 Ezagutu Lužice aneb Poznejte Lužici https://www.vybezek.eu/297720-ezagutu-luzice-aneb-poznejte-luzici/ Mon, 23 Nov 2026 18:23:04 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=297720 Literárně naučné miniturné po Čechách lužickosrbské spisovatelky Róži Domašcyny, básníka a překladatele Milana Hrabala a hudebníka Vojtěcha Kouby.

Ve dnech 3. a 4. listopadu 2026 proběhly dva večery věnované lužickosrbské literatuře a kultuře pod názvem Ezagutu Lužice (Poznejte Lužici), které pořádaly, ruku v ruce, nakladatelství Euskaldun a Společnost přátel Lužice. Nejednalo se o první takovou spolupráci, ale o vyvrcholení celého cyklu pořadů věnovaným menším jazykovým skupinám bez vlastní státnosti, které jsou nějakým způsobem svázány s českými zeměmi. První večer proběhl v Plzni v univerzitní kavárně Družba a následující den se přesunul takříkajíc na domácí hřiště do pražského Lužického semináře.

Hlavními hvězdami večerů byly Róža Domašcyna, jedna z nejvýznamnějších lužickosrbských autorek a Milan Hrabal, básník, překladatel, přítel a propagátor Lužice. O hudební doprovod se postaral Vojtěch Kouba, který představil publiku lužický folklór, ale zároveň i vlastní tvorbu.

Na první večer dorazilo asi čtyřicet zvídavých Plzeňanů, pro které bylo setkání s literaturou a historií nejmenšího západoslovanského národa iniciačním zážitkem. Milan Hrabal se ukázal, jako výborný průvodce lužicko-srbskými reáliemi i historií. Navíc bavil publikum tím, jak se postupně přiznával k různým překladatelským přehmatům. Poezie Róži Domašcyny a písně Vojtěcha Kouby vykouzlily čarovnou atmosféru jak v plzeňské studentské kavárně, tak pod barokní klenbou Lužického semináře.

Sychravé počasí za okny kontrastovalo s vřelou a neformální atmosférou obou večerů. U srdce zahřály i reakce návštěvníků. Etablovaný plzeňský básník Jan Sojka poklekl před organizátory večera na kolena, líbal jim ruce a děkoval za krásný večer. Herpetolog Ondřej Škach zase prohlásil, že nelituje toho, že vyměnil oslavu úspěšného odchovu zmije pavoučí v plzeňské ZOO, za lužickosrbský večer, neboť o zmijích ví všechno, ale o Lužici nevěděl doposud nic. Filolog Mikuláš Liptovský se nechal výkonem účinkujících dokonce strhnout ke slibu, že se na stará kolena pustí do studia sorabistiky. Studenty pražských uměleckých škol zase okouzlil Milan Hrabal natolik, že se zajímali o to, kdy bude mít v Lužickém semináři příští seminář o Lužici. Není divu, že se návštěvníci nechali vtáhnout do průběhu večera. Byl totiž úplně jiný, než obvykle literární večery bývají. Domašcyna s Hrabalem jsou na sebe mentálně navázaní a je na jejich vystoupení znát, že jsou sehraná dvojice. Kouba je pak skvěle doplňuje svými písněmi. Většina diváků slyšela asi poprvé dylanovku v lužické srbštině.  O pozitivních pocitech publika svědčí i ovace ve stoje, které následovaly po pražském večeru.

V době, kdy některé vlády vedou kulturní války proti vlastním občanům, tito se jim staví literaturou a radostí, kterou přináší umění slova. Je hezké vidět, když se lidé sejdou, aby vyslechli hlas malého národa a tím se o něco víc přiblížili ke břehům ostrova zapomenutých.

Martin Holý , Euskaldun
